classification.difficultyReason: Coordinates parity across the polynomial and two derivatives, then uses degree and monicity to determine coefficients from the two double roots. The preceding source supplies the same proof structure.

content.prompt: The polynomial $P(x)=x^4+px^2+q$ has a double root at $x=3$. Show that $x=-3$ is also a double root of $P(x)$. Hence find the values of $p$ and $q$.

answer.short: $P(-3)=P'(-3)=0$ and $P''(-3)\ne0$, so $-3$ is also a double root. Then $p=-18$ and $q=81$.
answer.worked:
$P$ is even, so $P(-3)=P(3)=0$.
$$\begin{align*}P'(x)&=4x^3+2px\\P'(-3)&=-P'(3)\\&=0\end{align*}$$
Also, $P''(x)=12x^2+2p$ is even. Since $3$ is a double root, $P''(3)\ne0$, and hence $P''(-3)=P''(3)\ne0$. Therefore $-3$ is also a double root.
The polynomial is monic and has degree four, so
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=(x-3)^2(x+3)^2\\&=(x^2-9)^2\\&=x^4-18x^2+81.\end{align*}$$
Comparing coefficients gives $p=-18$ and $q=81$.
